error_modes.label: Altitude control through the position change

texts.0: SP, due to back pressure released while unloading the aircraft to move aft and under the leader, did not hold the formation altitude during the position change. The result was a descent of more than 300 feet below the formation altitude, developed inside the crossing and not arrested. The IP took the controls to stop the sink and to reposition the aircraft in the formation.
texts.1: SP, due to a pitch input that was not coordinated with the power reduction, did not keep the formation altitude while crossing behind the leader. Altitude reached the 300 feet limit low, and the deviation stopped growing only after repeated verbal indications from the IP. The recovery to the formation altitude was slow and required a second prompt.
texts.2: SP, due to a power reduction applied without the matching pitch correction, did not hold altitude constant through the crossing. Altitude deviated between 150 and 300 feet below the formation altitude at the aft point of the maneuver. SP recognized the trend on the altimeter, corrected it in time and re-established the formation altitude without any intervention.
texts.3: SP held the formation altitude throughout the cross under, with deviation contained inside 150 feet. Pitch and power inputs were coordinated as the aircraft moved aft, across and back up into position. Any excursion was detected and corrected at once.
texts.4: SP completed the whole position change with negligible altitude excursion, effectively unchanged from the formation altitude and far inside the 150 feet band. Pitch control remained precise while the visual reference shifted from one side of the leader to the other, and no correction of the vertical position was needed after stabilization.
texts.marginal: SP stayed inside the altitude standards during the cross under, but on two crossings the deviation approached the tighter 150 feet band and always on the low side under the leader. The trend indicates that back pressure is relaxed as SP moves aft, and that the recovery of altitude is left to the end of the maneuver. Expected improvement is to hold the vertical position within a stable narrow band from the start to the completion of the crossing.

texts_at.1: SP let altitude sink to about 280 feet below the formation altitude at the aft point of the crossing, at the outer edge of the acceptable band, before the pitch and power inputs were coordinated. The excursion reached that far because pitch is still corrected after the power change rather than with it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to coordinate pitch with the power reduction from the start of the crossing so the sink stays smaller.
texts_at.2: SP let altitude sink to about 220 feet below the formation altitude, inside the acceptable band, before the trend was recognized on the altimeter and corrected in time. The deviation reached that far because the pitch correction followed the power change rather than accompanying it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to apply the pitch correction together with the power change so the sink stays smaller.
texts_at.3: SP held the deviation inside about 90 feet through the whole cross under, coordinating pitch and power as the aircraft moved aft, across and back into position. The small excursion that did appear followed a power reduction that was fractionally ahead of the matching pitch input. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to bring the pitch input into the power change at the same instant so the small excursion stops appearing.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the sink on the altimeter each time and held the deviation to about 220 feet, comfortably inside the acceptable band, correcting without any intervention. Coordinating the pitch input with the power reduction from the outset, rather than after the sink starts, would keep even that margin smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good altitude control.
texts_above.3: SP held the formation altitude within about 90 feet throughout the cross under, coordinating pitch and power as the aircraft moved aft, across and back into position, with any excursion detected and corrected at once. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good altitude control.
texts_above.4: SP completed the whole position change with altitude excursion of only a few tens of feet, effectively unchanged from the formation altitude, with pitch control remaining precise while the visual reference shifted from one side of the leader to the other. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent altitude control.

error_modes.label: Airspeed control during the aft displacement and the rejoin

texts.0: SP, due to a power reduction far larger than the one required to generate the aft displacement, did not control the airspeed during the position change. The result was a loss of more than 20 knots against the briefed formation airspeed and an uncontrolled drop well behind the leader. The IP intervened on the throttle and on the controls to recover the position.
texts.1: SP, due to a power correction applied only after the separation was already visible, did not keep the airspeed inside the formation band. The deviation reached 20 knots below the formation airspeed and was reduced only after verbal indications from the IP on the power setting. The rejoin to the new position was completed late.
texts.2: SP, due to a late reduction and a late restoration of power around the crossing, did not keep the airspeed constant during the position change. The deviation stayed between 10 and 20 knots from the formation airspeed. SP recognized the closure difference in good time, adjusted power and stabilized the airspeed without any intervention.
texts.3: SP controlled the airspeed inside 10 knots of the formation airspeed for the whole cross under. Power was reduced by the amount needed for the aft displacement and restored in time for the rejoin, so that closure remained controlled. Stabilization in the new position was achieved without airspeed hunting.
texts.4: SP flew the position change with negligible airspeed excursion, well inside the 10 knots band and with power inputs of the exact size required. The aft displacement, the crossing and the rejoin were flown with a continuously matched closure rate. No airspeed correction was necessary after the new position was reached.
texts.marginal: SP kept the airspeed inside the standards during the cross under, but the deviation repeatedly approached 10 knots low on the aft displacement. The trend is toward an initial power reduction slightly larger than needed, which is then compensated at the rejoin. Expected improvement is to size the power reduction so that the airspeed variation remains small and symmetrical about the formation airspeed.

texts_at.1: SP let airspeed decay to about 18 knots below the formation airspeed before the power correction was applied. The deviation reached that far because the correction still follows the visible separation rather than the throttle setting used to create it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to size the power correction to the displacement itself rather than to the resulting separation.
texts_at.2: SP let airspeed decay to about 14 knots below the formation airspeed, inside the acceptable band, before the difference was recognized in good time and power adjusted to stabilize it without any intervention. The deviation reached that far because the late reduction and the late restoration of power were both a beat behind the crossing. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to time the power changes with the crossing itself rather than with the closure it produces.
texts_at.3: SP controlled airspeed inside about 7 knots of the formation airspeed for the whole cross under, reducing power by the amount needed for the aft displacement and restoring it in time for the rejoin. The small variation that did appear followed a power change that was fractionally larger than the displacement required. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to size the power change more finely so the small variation stops appearing.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the closure difference in good time and held the deviation to about 14 knots, comfortably inside the acceptable band, adjusting power and stabilizing airspeed without any intervention. Timing the power changes with the crossing itself, rather than with the closure it produces, would keep even that margin smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound airspeed control.
texts_above.3: SP controlled airspeed inside about 7 knots of the formation airspeed for the whole cross under, reducing power by the amount needed for the aft displacement and restoring it in time for the rejoin so closure remained controlled throughout. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed airspeed control.
texts_above.4: SP flew the position change with negligible airspeed excursion, well inside the acceptable band, with power inputs of the exact size required so the aft displacement, the crossing and the rejoin were flown with a continuously matched closure rate. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional airspeed control.

error_modes.label: Heading on completion of the crossing

texts.0: SP, due to a bank input toward the new side that was not removed once the lateral displacement had been achieved, did not stabilize on the leader's heading at the completion of the crossing. The result was a divergence of more than 10 degrees from the formation heading with continued lateral travel away from the leader. The IP intervened on the controls to stop the divergence and to re-establish the position.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed removal of the crossing bank, did not roll out on the formation heading at the end of the position change. The heading divergence reached 10 degrees and was reduced only after verbal indications from the IP. Alignment with the leader was regained late and with a second correction.
texts.2: SP, due to a rollout started after the aircraft had already reached the new lateral position, did not settle on the formation heading immediately. The divergence remained between 5 and 10 degrees. SP recognized the misalignment against the leader, corrected it promptly and stabilized on the formation heading without any intervention.
texts.3: SP completed the crossing aligned with the leader, with heading divergence contained inside 5 degrees. The bank used for the lateral displacement was removed at the correct point so that the aircraft arrived on the new side already tracking the formation heading. No further heading correction was required after stabilization.
texts.4: SP arrived in the new position with negligible heading divergence, effectively parallel to the leader and far inside the 5 degrees band. The lateral displacement was stopped exactly at the required point, and the aircraft tracked the formation heading from the moment of arrival. Lateral position remained constant without further inputs.
texts.marginal: SP finished the crossings inside the heading standards, but the divergence at the rollout repeatedly approached 5 degrees, always in the direction of travel. The trend indicates that the bank is held slightly beyond the point where the new lateral position has been reached. Expected improvement is to anticipate the rollout so that the aircraft arrives on the new side already aligned with the leader.

texts_at.1: SP finished the crossing about 9 degrees off the formation heading, at the outer edge of the acceptable band, before the divergence was reduced. The error reached that far because the crossing bank is still removed after the new lateral position is reached rather than as it is reached. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to remove the bank as the lateral position is achieved so the divergence stays smaller.
texts_at.2: SP finished the crossing about 7 degrees off the formation heading, inside the acceptable band, before the misalignment was recognized against the leader and corrected promptly without any intervention. The divergence reached that far because the rollout was started once the new lateral position was already reached rather than as it was being reached. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to begin the rollout as the lateral displacement develops rather than after it is complete.
texts_at.3: SP completed the crossing within about 3 degrees of the leader's heading, with the bank used for the lateral displacement removed at the correct point so the aircraft arrived already tracking the formation heading. The small divergence that did appear followed a rollout that was a fraction late. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to lead the rollout a moment earlier so the small divergence stops appearing.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the misalignment against the leader on every crossing and held the divergence to about 7 degrees, comfortably inside the acceptable band, correcting promptly without any intervention. Beginning the rollout as the lateral displacement develops, rather than after it is complete, would keep even that margin smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady heading control on the crossing.
texts_above.3: SP completed the crossing within about 3 degrees of the leader's heading on every occasion, removing the bank used for the lateral displacement at the correct point so the aircraft arrived already tracking the formation heading. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate heading control on the crossing.
texts_above.4: SP arrived in the new position with negligible heading divergence, effectively parallel to the leader, with the lateral displacement stopped exactly at the required point and the aircraft tracking the formation heading from the moment of arrival. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary heading control on the crossing.

error_modes.label: Timely and correct execution of the position change on the leader's command

texts.0: SP, due to distraction by a secondary cockpit task during a critical phase of flight, did not execute the position change timely and correctly on the leader's command. The result was an initiation of the crossing several seconds after the signal and in the wrong direction, with the aircraft displaced toward the leader instead of aft. The IP intervened on the controls to stop the movement and to complete the change of position.
texts.1: SP, due to distraction by radio traffic while established in the formation, did not begin the position change at the time required by the leader's command. The crossing was started only after repeated verbal indications from the IP and after the leader had already been established in the new configuration. The sequence was then flown correctly but out of phase with the flight.
texts.2: SP, due to a short lapse in the visual scan of the leader after the command, did not initiate the position change at the exact moment of the signal. The result was a delay of a few seconds at the start of the crossing. SP recognized the delay, executed the remaining sequence in the correct order and completed the change of position without any intervention.
texts.3: SP executed the position change timely and correctly on the leader's command, without any need for IP intervention. The signal was acknowledged and the aft displacement, the crossing and the rejoin were flown in the correct sequence. The new position was established within the expected time.
texts.4: SP executed every position change immediately on the leader's command and in the exact briefed sequence, with no prompting of any kind. The response to the signal was instantaneous and the crossing was completed in a single continuous movement. The result was a change of position that matched the leader's expectation without any correction.
texts.marginal: SP executed the position changes on the leader's command within standards, but the initiation was consistently one to two seconds behind the signal. The trend is toward waiting for confirmation of the command before acting, which lengthens the time spent in transit. Expected improvement is to respond to the leader's signal immediately and to keep the whole sequence continuous.

texts_at.1: SP began the position change about two seconds after the leader's command, at the outer edge of the acceptable delay, before the sequence was flown correctly. The delay reached that far because the response is still triggered by a second confirmation of the signal rather than by the signal itself. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to act on the first signal rather than waiting to confirm it.
texts_at.2: SP began the position change about one second after the leader's command, inside the acceptable delay, then executed the remaining sequence in the correct order without any intervention. The delay reached that far because a short visual check preceded the response rather than the response following the signal directly. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to shorten that check so the response follows the signal more directly.
texts_at.3: SP initiated the position change within a fraction of a second of the leader's command, executing the aft displacement, the crossing and the rejoin in the correct sequence. The small delay that did appear followed a visual check that is not yet fully automatic. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to make that check automatic so the small delay stops appearing.

texts_above.2: SP responded to the leader's command about one second after the signal, comfortably inside the acceptable delay, executing the remaining sequence in the correct order without any intervention. Acting on the first signal rather than confirming it first would keep even that short delay smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured response to the leader's command.
texts_above.3: SP initiated the position change within a fraction of a second of the leader's command on every occasion, executing the aft displacement, the crossing and the rejoin in the correct sequence with no need for IP intervention. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise response to the leader's command.
texts_above.4: SP executed every position change immediately on the leader's command and in the exact briefed sequence, with no prompting of any kind, so the response to the signal was instantaneous and the crossing was completed in a single continuous movement. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate response to the leader's command.

error_modes.label: Longitudinal spacing within one aircraft length

texts.0: SP, due to a closure rate that was not controlled with small power corrections during the aft displacement, did not keep the spacing from the leader inside one aircraft length. The result was a separation of several aircraft lengths, with the leader's aspect no longer usable as a formation reference. The IP took the controls to re-establish the position.
texts.1: SP, due to power corrections applied only after the separation had become visible, did not hold the spacing within the required limit. Distance from the leader reached one aircraft length during the crossing and was reduced only after verbal indications from the IP. The rejoin to the new position was completed late and with excessive closure.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial power reduction slightly larger than required for the displacement, did not keep the spacing constant through the crossing. The separation grew toward one aircraft length at the aft point of the maneuver. SP recognized the increasing aspect change in time, restored power and closed the spacing without any intervention.
texts.3: SP kept the spacing from the leader inside one aircraft length throughout the cross under. Power was used in small corrections so that the aft displacement remained the minimum needed to clear the leader. The new position was reached with the correct longitudinal reference established.
texts.4: SP maintained the spacing from the leader essentially constant and well inside one aircraft length for the whole position change. The aft displacement was limited to what was needed for clearance and was recovered without overshoot. The formation references remained continuously usable at every point of the crossing.
texts.marginal: SP remained within the spacing limit during the cross under, but on each crossing the separation approached one aircraft length before being closed. The trend is toward using distance rather than precise power control to secure clearance from the leader. Expected improvement is to keep the aft displacement small and to control it with early, small power corrections.

texts_at.1: SP let the spacing from the leader reach close to a full aircraft length, at the outer limit of the acceptable band, before the position was rejoined. The spacing opened that far because power corrections are still applied after the separation is already visible rather than as it develops. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to apply small power corrections as the separation begins to grow rather than once it is visible.
texts_at.2: SP let the spacing from the leader grow to about three-quarters of an aircraft length, inside the acceptable band, before the increasing aspect change was recognized in time and power restored to close it without any intervention. The spacing grew that far because the initial power reduction for the displacement was fractionally larger than the crossing required. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to size the initial power reduction more finely so the spacing stays smaller.
texts_at.3: SP kept the spacing from the leader to about half an aircraft length throughout the cross under, using small power corrections so the aft displacement stayed the minimum needed to clear the leader. The small variation that did appear followed a power correction that was applied a beat late. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to apply that correction a beat earlier so the small variation stops appearing.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the increasing aspect change in time on every crossing and held the spacing to about three-quarters of an aircraft length, comfortably inside the acceptable band, restoring power to close it without any intervention. Sizing the initial power reduction more finely, rather than correcting the spacing it produces, would keep even that margin smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent longitudinal spacing control.
texts_above.3: SP kept the spacing from the leader to about half an aircraft length throughout the cross under, using small power corrections so the aft displacement remained the minimum needed to clear the leader with the correct longitudinal reference established on arrival. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined longitudinal spacing control.
texts_above.4: SP maintained the spacing from the leader essentially constant and well inside one aircraft length for the whole position change, with the aft displacement limited to what was needed for clearance and recovered without overshoot. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless longitudinal spacing control.

error_modes.label: Avoidance of the leader's prop wash during the crossing

texts.0: SP, due to an insufficient step down when passing behind the leader, did not keep the aircraft clear of the leader's prop wash. The result was entry into the wash with an uncommanded roll and a loss of the visual reference on the leader. The IP took the controls to recover the aircraft and to re-establish separation from the formation.
texts.1: SP, due to a vertical displacement started only after the aircraft had begun to move aft, did not avoid the edge of the leader's prop wash. The aircraft was buffeted while crossing and the step down was increased only after verbal indications from the IP. The remaining crossing was completed with delay and with the reference on the leader partly lost.
texts.2: SP, due to a step down established slightly late relative to the aft displacement, did not maintain the full vertical clearance from the leader's wake. The result was a brief light buffet at the closest point of the crossing. SP recognized the indication at once, increased the step down and completed the crossing clear of the wash without any intervention.
texts.3: SP kept the aircraft clear of the leader's prop wash for the whole position change. The step down was established before the aft displacement and was held until the aircraft was clear on the new side. No buffet was encountered and the visual reference on the leader was retained throughout.
texts.4: SP crossed under the leader with a vertical clearance that was correct and stable at every point, and no trace of wake was encountered. The step down was established early, held exactly as needed and recovered smoothly on arrival in the new position. The reference on the leader was maintained continuously and the crossing was flown in one uninterrupted movement.
texts.marginal: SP avoided the leader's prop wash on all crossings, but the step down was established only marginally before the aft displacement began. The trend is toward a vertical clearance that is adequate rather than comfortable at the closest point of the crossing. Expected improvement is to set the step down earlier and to hold it constant until the aircraft is fully clear on the new side.

texts_at.1: SP established the step down only about a second before the aft displacement began, at the outer edge of the acceptable margin, and was buffeted while crossing before the reference on the leader was regained. The margin reached that thin point because the step down is still triggered by the start of the lateral movement rather than set ahead of it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to set the step down before the aft displacement begins rather than with it.
texts_at.2: SP established the step down about a second before the aft displacement began, inside the acceptable margin, and felt a brief light buffet at the closest point before increasing the step down and completing the crossing clear of the wash without any intervention. The margin stayed that thin because the step down is still set relative to the start of the displacement rather than well ahead of it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to build in two to three seconds of margin before the displacement begins.
texts_at.3: SP established the step down with two to three seconds of margin before the aft displacement began on every crossing, so no buffet was encountered and the visual reference on the leader was retained throughout. The small margin that was used followed a step down that was set close to, rather than well ahead of, the displacement. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to build in a larger margin so the step down is never close to the displacement itself.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the buffet indication at once on every crossing and re-established a step down with about a second of margin, comfortably clear of the leader's wake, increasing it in time to complete the crossing without any intervention. Setting the step down well ahead of the aft displacement, rather than with it, would keep even that margin more comfortable. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound wake-avoidance technique.
texts_above.3: SP established the step down with two to three seconds of margin before the aft displacement began on every crossing, so no buffet was encountered and the visual reference on the leader was retained throughout the position change. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed wake-avoidance technique.
texts_above.4: SP crossed under the leader with a vertical clearance that was correct and stable at every point, with the step down established early, held exactly as needed and recovered smoothly on arrival, so no trace of wake was encountered on any crossing. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional wake-avoidance technique.

error_modes.label: Minimum separation of 10 feet from No1

texts.0: SP, due to a perceptual error in judging closure and lateral separation, did not respect the minimum distance from No1 during the crossing. The result was an approach closer than 10 feet to the leader with continuing closure and no corrective input. The IP took the controls to open the separation and to terminate the maneuver.
texts.1: SP, due to a perceptual error in judging closure while the leader's aspect was changing, did not keep the separation from No1 at a safe value. The distance reached the 10 feet limit and was opened only after an immediate verbal call from the IP. The position change was then completed with the reference on the leader regained late.
texts.2: SP, due to a misjudged closure rate at the start of the lateral displacement, did not maintain the planned separation from No1. The distance reduced noticeably toward the leader before stabilizing well above 10 feet. SP recognized the closure early, arrested it with a small lateral correction and completed the crossing without any intervention.
texts.3: SP kept the separation from No1 comfortably greater than 10 feet at every point of the position change. Closure was controlled with small, early inputs and the lateral displacement was stopped exactly where required. The crossing was completed with the safety margin from the leader preserved throughout.
texts.4: SP flew the whole position change with a separation from No1 that was never in question, far above the 10 feet minimum and constant at every phase. Closure was anticipated rather than corrected, and the aircraft was placed in the new position with a steady lateral margin. No convergence toward the leader developed at any stage.
texts.marginal: SP kept the separation from No1 above the minimum on every crossing, but the lateral margin reduced more than necessary at the point of passing under the leader. The trend indicates that the closure is judged late and then stopped with a single correction. Expected improvement is to assess the closure rate earlier so that the lateral margin remains comfortable and constant during the crossing.

texts_at.1: SP let the distance from No1 narrow to about 11 feet, barely above the 10 foot minimum, before the closure was opened after an immediate verbal call. The margin thinned that far because closure is still judged from the leader's aspect as a whole rather than from its rate of change. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to read the closure rate rather than the aspect alone so the margin above the minimum stays larger.
texts_at.2: SP let the distance from No1 reduce noticeably toward about 15 feet before the closure was recognized early and arrested with a small lateral correction without any intervention. The margin thinned that far because the closure rate at the start of the lateral displacement was misjudged by a small amount. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to assess the closure rate before the displacement starts rather than as it develops.
texts_at.3: SP kept the separation from No1 above about 18 feet at every point of the position change, controlling closure with small, early inputs so the lateral displacement stopped exactly where required. The small reduction that did appear followed a closure rate that was assessed a beat later than ideal. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to assess the closure rate a beat earlier so the small reduction stops appearing.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the closure early on every crossing and held the separation from No1 to about 15 feet, comfortably above the 10 foot minimum, arresting it with a small lateral correction without any intervention. Assessing the closure rate before the displacement starts, rather than as it develops, would keep even that margin more comfortable. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good separation discipline.
texts_above.3: SP kept the separation from No1 above about 18 feet at every point of the position change, controlling closure with small, early inputs so the lateral displacement stopped exactly where required with the safety margin from the leader preserved throughout. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good separation discipline.
texts_above.4: SP flew the whole position change with a separation from No1 that was never in question, far above the 10 foot minimum and constant at every phase, with closure anticipated rather than corrected. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent separation discipline.

error_modes.label: Smooth, continuous and solid aircraft control

texts.0: SP, due to an over-controlled aircraft (AE104) in the correction, did not control the aircraft in a smooth, continuous and solid manner during the cross under. The result was a sustained lateral oscillation about the intended path, with successive inputs that amplified rather than damped the movement. The IP took the controls to stabilize the aircraft and to establish it in the new position.
texts.1: SP, due to control inputs of excessive size applied in response to each visual change, did not fly the position change smoothly and continuously. The aircraft moved in a series of abrupt steps and the oscillation stopped only after verbal indications from the IP on the size of the inputs. Stabilization in the new position was reached late.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial control input larger than the displacement required, did not keep the movement continuous at the start of the crossing. The result was an abrupt beginning followed by a small overshoot of the intended path. SP reduced the size of the subsequent inputs, damped the movement and completed the crossing smoothly without any intervention.
texts.3: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth, continuous and solid manner throughout the position change. Control inputs were proportionate to the displacement required and the aircraft moved along one continuous path from the old to the new position. No overshoot or oscillation developed at any stage.
texts.4: SP flew the position change as a single continuous movement, with control inputs so measured that no correction of the path was necessary. The aircraft was placed in the new position with a positive, solid stop and no residual oscillation. Control precision was maintained even while the visual reference on the leader changed side.
texts.marginal: SP flew the cross under within the control standards, but each crossing began with an input slightly larger than needed and was followed by a small damping correction. The trend indicates a step-wise rather than a continuous displacement. Expected improvement is to size the initial input to the required displacement so that the aircraft moves along one smooth path and stops positively in the new position.

texts_at.1: SP let the path depart the intended line by about 3 feet before the oscillation was damped and the aircraft stabilized in the new position. The departure reached that far because the control inputs are still sized for the whole displacement rather than proportioned to it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to proportion each input to the displacement remaining so the departure stays smaller.
texts_at.2: SP let the path depart the intended line by about 2 feet on the initial input before the size of the subsequent inputs was reduced and the movement damped without any intervention. The departure reached that far because the first control input was sized larger than the displacement required. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to size the first input to the displacement itself rather than to a fixed correction.
texts_at.3: SP kept the path within about 1 foot of the intended line for the whole position change, with control inputs proportionate to the displacement required so the aircraft moved along one continuous path. The small departure that did appear followed an input that was fractionally larger than needed. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to size that input more finely so the small departure stops appearing.

texts_above.2: SP reduced the size of each subsequent input as soon as an overshoot appeared and kept the path within about 2 feet of the intended line, comfortably inside the acceptable band, completing every crossing smoothly without any intervention. Sizing the first input to the displacement itself, rather than to a fixed correction, would keep even that margin smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady aircraft control through the crossing.
texts_above.3: SP controlled the aircraft in a smooth, continuous and solid manner throughout the position change, with control inputs proportionate to the displacement required so the path stayed within about 1 foot of the intended line and no overshoot or oscillation developed. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate aircraft control through the crossing.
texts_above.4: SP flew the position change as a single continuous movement, with control inputs so measured that no correction of the path was necessary, placing the aircraft in the new position with a positive, solid stop and no residual oscillation. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary aircraft control through the crossing.

error_modes.label: Establishing the small forward LOS rate that starts the aft displacement

texts.0: SP, due to the initial power reduction being omitted at the start of the cross under, did not establish the small forward LOS rate that produces the aft displacement. The lateral movement toward the new side was begun from the fingertip position with no nose-tail clearance built up, and the aircraft was allowed to approach No1 closer than 10 feet while still nearly abeam. The IP took the controls to stop the lateral movement and to open the separation from the leader.
texts.1: SP, due to a power reduction too small to generate any usable forward LOS rate, did not move aft before starting to cross behind the leader. Separation from No1 reduced to the 10 feet limit with the leader still abeam, and the aft displacement was created only after verbal indications from the IP on the throttle. The crossing was completed late and with the clearance regained rather than planned.
texts.2: SP, due to a power reduction applied after the lateral movement had already started, established the small forward LOS rate late in the sequence. Nose-tail clearance was therefore still building while the aircraft was moving toward the leader, and the spacing gained aft stayed below the intended one aircraft length reference. SP recognized the leader's aspect, held the lateral movement until clearance was achieved and completed the crossing without any intervention.
texts.3: SP reduced power as required to establish a small forward LOS rate before any lateral movement was made. The aft displacement developed first, so that the crossing behind the leader was flown with spacing inside one aircraft length and with separation from No1 clearly greater than 10 feet. The sequence of aft displacement, crossing and rejoin was flown in the correct order.
texts.4: SP established a forward LOS rate of exactly the size needed, using a power reduction of a few percent torque, and let the aft displacement build before any bank was applied. Nose-tail clearance was achieved with negligible loss of the formation reference and the separation from No1 never came near the 10 feet minimum. No further adjustment of the longitudinal position was required during the crossing.
texts.marginal: SP produced a forward LOS rate on each cross under, but on repeated attempts the lateral movement was started while the aft displacement was still developing. Spacing and separation remained inside the standards, yet the clearance behind the leader was consistently at the low end of what the technique calls for. Expected improvement is to reduce power first, let the small forward LOS rate build the nose-tail clearance, and only then begin the lateral displacement.

texts_at.1: SP let separation from No1 narrow to about 11 feet before the forward LOS rate needed to build clearance was established. The separation thinned that far because the power reduction that starts the LOS rate is still sized too small to build clearance ahead of the lateral movement. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to size the initial power reduction to build the LOS rate before any lateral movement is made.
texts_at.2: SP built the aft displacement to about three-quarters of an aircraft length before the lateral movement was allowed to continue, with the power reduction applied slightly after the lateral movement had already started. The clearance stayed that far short of the intended one aircraft length reference because the power reduction lagged the start of the lateral movement. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to reduce power before starting the lateral movement rather than after it.
texts_at.3: SP built the aft displacement to about half an aircraft length with separation held near 20 feet before any lateral movement was made, flying the aft displacement, crossing and rejoin in the correct order. The small variation that did appear followed a power reduction that was fractionally later than ideal. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to reduce power a moment earlier so the small variation stops appearing.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the leader's aspect on every cross under and held the lateral movement until clearance reached about three-quarters of an aircraft length, comfortably inside the intended reference, completing the crossing without any intervention. Reducing power before the lateral movement starts, rather than after it, would keep even that margin larger. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound LOS-rate technique.
texts_above.3: SP reduced power as required to establish a small forward LOS rate before any lateral movement was made, so the aft displacement built to about half an aircraft length with separation held near 20 feet and the crossing flown in the correct order. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed LOS-rate technique.
texts_above.4: SP established a forward LOS rate of exactly the size needed and let the aft displacement build before any bank was applied, so nose-tail clearance was achieved with negligible loss of the formation reference and separation from No1 never came near the 10 foot minimum. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional LOS-rate technique.

error_modes.label: Sizing the power reduction when the cross under is flown in a climb

texts.0: SP, due to a full-sized power reduction applied while the formation was climbing, did not limit the rearward movement generated during the cross under. Excessive rearward movement developed, the aircraft fell several aircraft lengths behind the leader and the airspeed dropped more than 20 knots below the formation airspeed with no timely power restoration. The IP took the controls and restored power to arrest the separation.
texts.1: SP, due to a power reduction not adapted to the climb, allowed excessive rearward movement during the position change. The aircraft moved beyond one aircraft length aft and the airspeed reached 20 knots below the formation airspeed, with the trend stopped only after verbal indications from the IP. The rejoin to the new side was completed well behind the expected timing.
texts.2: SP, due to a power reduction sized as for level flight while the formation was climbing, generated more rearward movement than the crossing required. Airspeed decayed between 10 and 20 knots below the formation airspeed and the spacing approached one aircraft length. SP recognized the growing separation on the leader's aspect, restored power in time and completed the crossing without any intervention.
texts.3: SP kept the power reduction small during the cross under in the climb, so that the rearward movement stayed no larger than the crossing required. Spacing remained inside one aircraft length and the airspeed deviation stayed inside 10 knots of the formation airspeed. Power was restored at the correct point to stop the aft travel.
texts.4: SP adapted the power reduction to the climb without prompting, using a reduction of only a few percent torque, and the rearward movement remained just sufficient for nose-tail clearance. Airspeed excursion was negligible against the formation airspeed and the spacing stayed well inside one aircraft length. The crossing in the climb was flown with no perceptible change of closure.
texts.marginal: SP completed the cross unders in the climb inside the standards, but the rearward movement was repeatedly larger than needed, with airspeed approaching 10 knots low. The trend indicates that the same power reduction is used regardless of whether the formation is level or climbing. Expected improvement is to keep the power reduction small whenever the cross under is flown in a climb, so that the aft displacement stays at the minimum required.

texts_at.1: SP let airspeed reach about 18 knots below the formation airspeed with spacing close to a full aircraft length before power was restored. The deviation reached that far because the power reduction used for the cross under is still sized as for level flight rather than adjusted for the climb. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to size the power reduction to the climb itself so the deviation stays smaller.
texts_at.2: SP let airspeed decay to about 14 knots below the formation airspeed with spacing approaching three-quarters of an aircraft length before the growing separation was recognized on the leader's aspect and power restored in time without any intervention. The deviation reached that far because the power reduction sized for level flight generated more rearward movement than the climb required. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to reduce the power setting used whenever the cross under is flown in a climb.
texts_at.3: SP kept airspeed within about 7 knots of the formation airspeed with spacing to about half an aircraft length, keeping the power reduction small during the cross under in the climb so the rearward movement stayed no larger than the crossing required. The small variation that did appear followed a power setting that was fractionally larger than the climb required. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to reduce the power setting slightly further so the small variation stops appearing.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the growing separation on the leader's aspect and restored power in time to hold airspeed to about 14 knots low with spacing near three-quarters of an aircraft length, comfortably inside the acceptable band, without any intervention. Sizing the power reduction to the climb from the outset, rather than as for level flight, would keep even that margin smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid power sizing in the climb.
texts_above.3: SP kept the power reduction small during the cross under in the climb, so the rearward movement stayed no larger than the crossing required, with spacing remaining inside about half an aircraft length and airspeed deviation inside about 7 knots. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed power sizing in the climb.
texts_above.4: SP adapted the power reduction to the climb without prompting, using a reduction of only a few percent torque, so the rearward movement remained just sufficient for nose-tail clearance with negligible airspeed excursion. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding power sizing in the climb.

error_modes.label: Anticipating the power addition required while crossing behind No1

texts.0: SP, due to failing to anticipate the slight power increase normally required while flying across and behind the leader, did not stop the rearward movement once nose-tail clearance had been achieved. The aircraft continued to fall aft through the crossing, ending several aircraft lengths behind with more than 20 knots of airspeed difference from the formation and no usable reference on No1. The IP took the controls to restore power and to rejoin the formation.
texts.1: SP, due to power being added only after the rearward travel was already obvious, did not maintain proper nose-tail separation while crossing behind the leader. The spacing opened to the one aircraft length limit and the airspeed to 20 knots below the formation airspeed, and the trend was arrested only after verbal indications from the IP. The rejoin required a large power addition and a late catch-up.
texts.2: SP, due to reacting to the rearward movement instead of anticipating the power change, did not hold the nose-tail separation constant through the crossing. Spacing drifted toward one aircraft length and airspeed between 10 and 20 knots below the formation airspeed while the aircraft was behind the leader. SP identified the growing distance in good time, added power and re-established the correct separation without any intervention.
texts.3: SP anticipated each power change during the cross under, adding power slightly to stop the rearward movement and again as required while crossing behind the leader. Nose-tail separation stayed at the value established at the start, with spacing inside one aircraft length and airspeed inside 10 knots of the formation airspeed. No large throttle movements were needed at any point.
texts.4: SP anticipated the power changes so precisely that the nose-tail separation remained visibly constant from the moment clearance was established until the rejoin. Airspeed excursion against the formation airspeed was negligible and spacing stayed well inside one aircraft length throughout the crossing. Throttle inputs were small, early and continuous rather than corrective.
texts.marginal: SP maintained nose-tail separation inside the standards, but the power addition behind the leader was repeatedly made after the aft movement had started to grow. Spacing approached one aircraft length on several crossings before power was restored. Expected improvement is to anticipate the slight power increase required while crossing behind No1, so that the separation established at the start is simply held rather than recovered.

texts_at.1: SP let the spacing open to about a full aircraft length and airspeed reach about 18 knots below the formation airspeed before power was added and the trend was arrested. The spacing opened that far because power is still added after the rearward travel is obvious rather than anticipated. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to anticipate the power change as clearance is achieved rather than after the aircraft has fallen well aft.
texts_at.2: SP let the spacing drift toward about three-quarters of an aircraft length with airspeed about 14 knots below the formation airspeed before the growing distance was identified in good time and power added to re-establish the correct separation without any intervention. The spacing drifted that far because the aircraft was still reacting to the rearward movement rather than anticipating the power change required to stop it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to anticipate the power change at the point clearance is achieved rather than react to the drift it produces.
texts_at.3: SP kept nose-tail separation at about half an aircraft length with airspeed within about 7 knots of the formation airspeed, anticipating each power change during the cross under so no large throttle movement was needed at any point. The small variation that did appear followed a power addition that was fractionally later than ideal. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to anticipate that addition a moment earlier so the small variation stops appearing.

texts_above.2: SP identified the growing distance in good time on every crossing and held spacing to about three-quarters of an aircraft length with airspeed about 14 knots below the formation airspeed, comfortably inside the acceptable band, adding power to re-establish separation without any intervention. Anticipating the power change at the point clearance is achieved, rather than reacting to the drift it produces, would keep even that margin smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady power anticipation behind the leader.
texts_above.3: SP anticipated each power change during the cross under, adding power slightly to stop the rearward movement and again as required while crossing behind the leader, so nose-tail separation stayed at the value established at the start with spacing inside about half an aircraft length. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate power anticipation behind the leader.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated the power changes so precisely that the nose-tail separation remained visibly constant from the moment clearance was established until the rejoin, with airspeed excursion negligible throughout the crossing. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary power anticipation behind the leader.

error_modes.label: Size of the bank used to create the heading crossing angle

texts.0: SP, due to a large bank change instead of the slight bank needed to create a small HCA, did not control the rate of lateral travel across to the new side. The heading diverged more than 10 degrees from the leader's heading and the aircraft continued to translate laterally well past the intended position on the new side. The IP took the controls to remove the crossing angle and to stop the lateral travel.
texts.1: SP, due to a bank input well beyond the few degrees of heading change the technique calls for, generated an excessive HCA during the cross under. Heading divergence reached 10 degrees and the lateral travel had to be stopped after verbal indications from the IP. The arrival on the new side was achieved only after an opposite correction of similar size.
texts.2: SP, due to a bank larger than required to set a small HCA, crossed to the new side with a lateral rate higher than intended. Heading divergence stayed between 5 and 10 degrees and the aircraft reached the new position with residual lateral movement. SP recognized the excess rate, reduced the crossing angle in time and stabilized without any intervention.
texts.3: SP used a slight bank toward the new side, changing heading by only a few degrees to create a small HCA, then rolled wings-level to fly across and behind the leader. Heading divergence stayed inside 5 degrees and the lateral travel was controlled and predictable. The new position was reached without an opposite correction.
texts.4: SP created an HCA of only a few degrees, exactly matched to the lateral distance to be covered, and the crossing developed as one continuous and unhurried translation. Heading divergence from the formation heading was negligible and the aircraft stopped laterally exactly on the new position. Pitch and bank changes remained small throughout.
texts.marginal: SP kept the crossing angles inside the standards, but the initial bank was repeatedly larger than the small HCA the technique describes, with divergence approaching 5 degrees. The result each time was a lateral rate that had to be reduced before arrival on the new side. Expected improvement is to make small pitch and bank changes and to size the HCA to the lateral distance actually required.

texts_at.1: SP generated a heading divergence of about 9 degrees before the lateral travel was stopped after an opposite correction of similar size. The divergence reached that far because the bank used to set the crossing angle is still sized well beyond the few degrees the technique calls for. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to size the bank to the small crossing angle the technique describes so the divergence stays smaller.
texts_at.2: SP generated a heading divergence of about 7 degrees before the excess rate was recognized and the crossing angle reduced in time to stabilize without any intervention. The divergence reached that far because the bank used was larger than required to set a small crossing angle. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to size the initial bank to the small crossing angle required rather than reduce it after the rate is excessive.
texts_at.3: SP used a slight bank toward the new side, changing heading by only a few degrees, and kept the divergence within about 3 degrees while the lateral travel remained controlled and predictable. The small divergence that did appear followed a bank input that was fractionally larger than the crossing angle required. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to size that bank input more finely so the small divergence stops appearing.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the excess lateral rate on every crossing and held the heading divergence to about 7 degrees, comfortably inside the acceptable band, reducing the crossing angle in time to stabilize without any intervention. Sizing the initial bank to the small crossing angle the technique calls for, rather than reducing an excess rate afterward, would keep even that margin smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured bank sizing for the crossing angle.
texts_above.3: SP used a slight bank toward the new side on every crossing, changing heading by only a few degrees to create a small crossing angle, then rolled wings-level to fly across and behind the leader, keeping divergence inside about 3 degrees with the lateral travel controlled and predictable. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise bank sizing for the crossing angle.
texts_above.4: SP created a crossing angle of only a few degrees, exactly matched to the lateral distance to be covered, so the crossing developed as one continuous and unhurried translation with negligible heading divergence from the formation heading. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate bank sizing for the crossing angle.

error_modes.label: Use of the canopy bow on the elevator trailing edge as nose-tail reference

texts.0: SP, due to not using the nose-tail reference of the canopy bow superimposed on the trailing edge of No1's elevator, did not verify the clearance before moving back and down below the leader's POM. The crossing was started with the aircraft still displaced forward of that reference and the separation from No1 reduced to less than 10 feet during the lateral travel. The IP took the controls to open the separation and to re-establish the position.
texts.1: SP, due to judging the nose-tail position on general impression rather than on the canopy bow and elevator trailing edge reference, crossed behind the leader with less clearance than the technique requires. The separation from No1 reached the 10 feet limit and was opened only after verbal indications from the IP. The aircraft was repositioned below the leader's POM late in the sequence.
texts.2: SP, due to checking the canopy bow against the elevator trailing edge only after the crossing had begun, moved back and down below the leader's POM with the clearance not yet confirmed. The separation from No1 remained above 10 feet but with less margin than intended and the crossing had to be slowed. SP re-established the reference in good time and completed the position change without any intervention.
texts.3: SP established the nose-tail reference before crossing, with the canopy bow appearing superimposed on the trailing edge of No1's elevator, and moved back and down below the leader's POM. The clearance was confirmed visually before any lateral travel and the separation from No1 stayed clearly greater than 10 feet. The crossing was flown with the reference held stable.
texts.4: SP used the canopy bow on the elevator trailing edge as a continuous reference, so that the nose-tail geometry was known at every point of the cross under. Clearance below the leader's POM was established first and the separation from No1 remained far greater than the 10 feet minimum. The reference was regained immediately on the new side with no re-assessment needed.
texts.marginal: SP crossed with acceptable clearance, but the canopy bow was repeatedly only approximately aligned with No1's elevator trailing edge before the lateral travel began. Separation stayed inside the standards while the margin behind the leader was consistently on the small side. Expected improvement is to confirm the nose-tail reference explicitly before moving back and down below the leader's POM on every cross under.

texts_at.1: SP crossed behind the leader with separation from No1 reaching about 11 feet before the nose-tail reference was properly established and the aircraft repositioned below the leader's plane of motion. The margin thinned that far because the position was judged on general impression before the canopy bow and elevator trailing edge reference was checked. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to check the nose-tail reference before crossing rather than after the margin has already thinned.
texts_at.2: SP moved back and down below the leader's plane of motion with clearance about 15 feet before the reference was re-established in good time and the position change completed without any intervention. The margin thinned that far because the canopy bow was checked against the elevator trailing edge only after the crossing had begun. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to check the reference before the crossing starts rather than during it.
texts_at.3: SP established the nose-tail reference before crossing, with the canopy bow appearing superimposed on the trailing edge of No1's elevator, and kept separation from No1 at about 18 feet throughout. The small reduction that did appear followed a reference check that was a beat later than ideal. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to check that reference a beat earlier so the small reduction stops appearing.

texts_above.2: SP re-established the nose-tail reference in good time on every crossing and held separation from No1 to about 15 feet, comfortably above the 10 foot minimum, completing the position change without any intervention. Checking the reference before the crossing starts, rather than during it, would keep even that margin more comfortable. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable nose-tail reference technique.
texts_above.3: SP established the nose-tail reference before crossing, with the canopy bow appearing superimposed on the trailing edge of No1's elevator, confirming clearance visually before any lateral travel so separation from No1 stayed at about 18 feet with the reference held stable. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good nose-tail reference technique.
texts_above.4: SP used the canopy bow on the elevator trailing edge as a continuous reference, so the nose-tail geometry was known at every point of the cross under and separation from No1 remained far greater than the 10 foot minimum. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior nose-tail reference technique.

error_modes.label: Power reduction on arrival in the position on the new side

texts.0: SP, due to a late power reduction after adding power to move forward and up into position, did not stabilize on the new side and overshot the position. The aircraft continued forward and up through the formation reference, closing to less than 10 feet from No1 and climbing more than 300 feet above the formation altitude before the movement was arrested. The IP took the controls to stop the closure and to re-establish the formation position.
texts.1: SP, due to leaving the power addition in beyond the point where the position was reached, did not arrest the forward and upward movement at the correct time. The aircraft went through the position with closure toward No1 and a climb reaching 300 feet above the formation altitude, reduced only after verbal indications from the IP. Stabilization on the new side required a second correction in both power and pitch.
texts.2: SP, due to a power reduction applied after arrival instead of just before it, ended the crossing with residual forward and upward movement. The overshoot in the vertical stayed between 150 and 300 feet above the formation altitude and the closure toward No1 had to be stopped. SP recognized the movement, reduced power and settled into the position in time without any intervention.
texts.3: SP added power to move forward and up into the new position and reduced power in time to stabilize there. The arrival was contained inside 150 feet of the formation altitude with separation from No1 well above 10 feet and no forward overshoot. The position was held from the moment of arrival.
texts.4: SP timed the power reduction so that the aircraft arrived in the position with the residual movement already zero. Vertical excursion at arrival was negligible against the formation altitude and the lateral and longitudinal references were correct at the first attempt. No further throttle correction was required after stabilization on the new side.
texts.marginal: SP stabilized on the new side inside the standards, but the power reduction was repeatedly made at arrival rather than in anticipation of it. Each crossing ended with a small forward and upward overshoot that had to be taken out, with vertical excursion approaching 150 feet. Expected improvement is to begin the power reduction before the position is reached, so that the aircraft arrives already stabilized.

texts_at.1: SP went through the position with a climb reaching about 280 feet above the formation altitude and closure toward No1, before the movement was arrested by a second correction. The overshoot reached that far because the power reduction is still applied after arrival rather than in anticipation of it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to begin the power reduction before the position is reached so the overshoot stays smaller.
texts_at.2: SP ended the crossing with residual forward and upward movement reaching about 220 feet above the formation altitude before the movement was recognized and power reduced to settle into position in time without any intervention. The overshoot reached that far because the power reduction was applied after arrival instead of just before it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to apply the power reduction just before arrival rather than at it.
texts_at.3: SP added power to move forward and up into the new position and reduced power in time to stabilize there, containing the arrival inside about 90 feet of the formation altitude with separation from No1 well above 10 feet. The small overshoot that did appear followed a power reduction that was a fraction late. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to apply that reduction a fraction earlier so the small overshoot stops appearing.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the residual movement each time and reduced power to settle the arrival within about 220 feet of the formation altitude, comfortably inside the acceptable band, without any intervention. Applying the power reduction just before arrival, rather than at it, would keep even that margin smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid arrival power technique.
texts_above.3: SP added power to move forward and up into the new position and reduced power in time to stabilize there, containing the arrival inside about 90 feet of the formation altitude with separation from No1 well above 10 feet and no forward overshoot. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed arrival power technique.
texts_above.4: SP timed the power reduction so the aircraft arrived in the position with the residual movement already zero, with vertical excursion at arrival negligible against the formation altitude and the lateral and longitudinal references correct at the first attempt. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding arrival power technique.

error_modes.label: Nose-tail separation while inspecting No1 during the BD check crossunder

texts.0: SP, due to attention being concentrated on the inspection for damage, leaks and missing panels, did not maintain nose-tail separation while crossing under to the other side of No1. The aircraft drifted forward out of the cleared geometry and approached No1 closer than 10 feet with the scan still on the leader's structure. The IP took the controls to open the separation and to terminate the check.
texts.1: SP, due to the inspection task displacing the formation scan, did not hold nose-tail separation during the BD check crossunder. The clearance behind the leader reduced to the 10 feet limit and was recovered only after verbal indications from the IP. The inspection of the second side had to be repeated after the position was re-established.
texts.2: SP, due to dwelling on the leader's wing while repositioning, allowed the nose-tail separation to reduce during the cross under of the BD check. The clearance remained above 10 feet but with a visibly reducing margin as the scan stayed on the inspection. SP interrupted the inspection, re-established the separation in time and completed the check without any intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained nose-tail separation throughout the BD check crossunder while inspecting No1 for damage, leaks, missing panels and irregularities. The scan alternated between the inspection and the formation references, so that spacing stayed inside one aircraft length and separation clearly above 10 feet. The check was completed on both sides and the original position was regained.
texts.4: SP inspected No1 in detail on both sides while the nose-tail geometry remained visibly constant throughout the repositioning. Separation was maintained far above the 10 feet minimum and the aircraft returned to the formation position from which the check was initiated with no correction required. The result of the check was passed without any degradation of the formation position.
texts.marginal: SP kept the separation inside the standards during the BD check, but the nose-tail margin reduced each time the inspection scan was held on the leader for longer periods. The position was always recovered, yet the trend shows the formation scan being suspended while inspecting. Expected improvement is to keep the inspection in short segments so that nose-tail separation is monitored continuously through the crossunder.

texts_at.1: SP let clearance behind the leader reduce to about 11 feet, at the limit of the acceptable band, before it was recovered after a verbal indication from the IP. The clearance thinned that far because the formation scan is still displaced entirely by the inspection task rather than shared with it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to keep the formation scan active alongside the inspection rather than suspending it.
texts_at.2: SP let the nose-tail separation reduce to about 15 feet, with a visibly narrowing margin, before the inspection was interrupted and the separation re-established in time without any intervention. The margin narrowed that far because the scan stayed on the leader's structure for longer than the inspection required. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to interrupt the inspection sooner so the margin does not narrow as far.
texts_at.3: SP maintained nose-tail separation at about 18 feet throughout the BD check crossunder, alternating the scan between the inspection and the formation references so spacing stayed inside one aircraft length. The small narrowing that did appear followed a scan interval that was a moment longer than ideal. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to shorten that interval so the small narrowing stops appearing.

texts_above.2: SP interrupted the inspection at the first indication of a narrowing margin and held nose-tail separation to about 15 feet, comfortably above the 10 foot minimum, re-establishing it in time without any intervention. Keeping the formation scan active alongside the inspection, rather than suspending it, would keep even that margin more comfortable. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent scan discipline during the BD check.
texts_above.3: SP maintained nose-tail separation throughout the BD check crossunder while inspecting No1 for damage, leaks, missing panels and irregularities, alternating the scan between the inspection and the formation references so spacing stayed inside one aircraft length at about 18 feet. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined scan discipline during the BD check.
texts_above.4: SP inspected No1 in detail on both sides while the nose-tail geometry remained visibly constant throughout the repositioning, with separation maintained far above the 10 foot minimum and no correction required on return to the original position. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless scan discipline during the BD check.

error_modes.label: Correcting excessive spacing that develops behind No1 after the crossing

texts.0: SP, due to attempting to correct excessive spacing forward with power alone from directly behind and below the leader, did not recognize the closure rate that developed. The aircraft came out of the excess spacing with an uncontrolled overtake and closed to less than 10 feet from No1 with no lateral offset from which to judge the closure. The IP took the controls to stop the overtake and to re-establish separation.
texts.1: SP, due to correcting the excessive spacing with power only, without establishing a small amount of lead pursuit in the turn, did not control the closure back into position. The separation from No1 reduced to the 10 feet limit before the overtake was arrested, and only after verbal indications from the IP. The final positioning was achieved with a large power reduction late in the correction.
texts.2: SP, due to relying mainly on power to close the excessive spacing from directly astern, recognized the closure rate later than required. The overtake had to be broken with a marked power reduction, with the separation from No1 reduced well below the intended margin although above 10 feet. SP established a lateral offset in time to judge the closure and completed the correction without any intervention.
texts.3: SP corrected the excessive spacing by adding power together with a small amount of lead pursuit in the turn, and by moving off to one side when wings-level to obtain a better visual perspective of No1. Closure was recognized early, the aircraft returned inside one aircraft length and the separation from No1 stayed well above 10 feet. The correction was completed with a single, controlled power cycle.
texts.4: SP treated the excessive spacing with the correct technique from the outset, combining a small power addition with a slight lead pursuit and a lateral perspective on No1. Closure was continuously visible and the return to position was made with negligible overtake and no reduction of the safety margin. The correct spacing was regained without any subsequent adjustment.
texts.marginal: SP recovered the correct spacing inside the standards, but the first correction was repeatedly attempted with power alone from directly astern before an offset was taken. Closure was recognized late on each occasion, leaving less margin than intended on the return to position. Expected improvement is to add power together with a small amount of lead pursuit, or to move off to one side when wings-level, whenever excessive spacing develops.

texts_at.1: SP let the overtake reduce separation from No1 to about 11 feet before it was arrested with a large, late power reduction. The separation thinned that far because the correction still relies on power alone from directly astern rather than on an offset that lets the closure be judged. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to move off to one side when wings-level so the closure can be judged and stopped earlier.
texts_at.2: SP let the separation from No1 reduce to about 15 feet, above 10 feet but below the intended margin, before an offset was established in time to judge the closure and the correction completed without any intervention. The margin thinned that far because the closure was recognized later than the aspect cues allowed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to establish the lateral offset earlier so closure is judged before the margin thins as far.
texts_at.3: SP corrected every spacing excursion by adding power together with a small amount of lead pursuit while the leader was turning, and by moving off to one side when wings-level, returning inside one aircraft length with separation from No1 at about 18 feet. The small reduction that did appear followed a correction that was a beat later than ideal. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to apply that correction a beat earlier so the small reduction stops appearing.

texts_above.2: SP established a lateral offset in time on every occasion and held separation from No1 to about 15 feet, comfortably above the 10 foot minimum, judging the closure and completing the correction without any intervention. Moving off to one side when wings-level from the outset, rather than relying on power alone, would keep even that margin more comfortable. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound spacing-recovery technique.
texts_above.3: SP corrected the excessive spacing by adding power together with a small amount of lead pursuit in the turn, and by moving off to one side when wings-level to obtain a better visual perspective of No1, returning inside one aircraft length with separation from No1 at about 18 feet. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed spacing-recovery technique.
texts_above.4: SP treated the excessive spacing with the correct technique from the outset, combining a small power addition with a slight lead pursuit and a lateral perspective on No1, so closure was continuously visible and the return to position was made with negligible overtake. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional spacing-recovery technique.
